story.t: Thought I'd stay in Linux? I'm going to hop VLANs and hijack your prefixes.
Switching and BGP: mistakes here take a lot of people down at once. Careful.

levels.title: VLAN hopping
levels.goal: Set the camera port as access and the uplink as a trunk hardened against VLAN hopping.
levels.intro: Camera on VLAN 30 on Gi1/0/10. Uplink to the core with only VLANs 10, 20 and 30. Native VLAN on an unused VLAN and no automatic negotiation.
levels.z: Your switch negotiates a trunk with anyone. I'll hop straight to the management VLAN.
levels.me: Access is access, trunk is trunk. And DTP off.
lesson: A VLAN splits one physical switch into several logical networks. A camera on VLAN 30 can't see who's on VLAN 10 without going through a router.
An access port belongs to a single VLAN: that's where hosts plug in (PC, camera, printer). A trunk port carries several VLANs tagged with 802.1Q: it's the link between switches.
DTP negotiates trunks on its own. If the port accepts negotiation, an attacker pretends to be a switch, forms a trunk and gets access to every VLAN. switchport nonegotiate turns that off.
The native VLAN travels untagged on the trunk. Putting it on a VLAN with no users (e.g. 999) prevents the double tagging attack.
allowed vlan limits the trunk to the VLANs that really need to cross it.
levels.tip: A host port is access. The uplink is a trunk with an explicit VLAN list. Unused native VLAN (e.g. 999) and nonegotiate turn DTP off.
levels.learn: VLAN hopping happens through switch spoofing (DTP forming a trunk with the attacker) or double tagging (abusing the native VLAN). Defense: host ports in fixed access, switchport nonegotiate, trunk with explicit allowed vlan and a native VLAN that carries no users.

explain.a: The camera is a host: access port, fixed to one VLAN.
explain.b: The camera goes on VLAN 30, as the mission asks.
explain.d: Only VLANs 10, 20 and 30 pass. The others stay off the trunk.
explain.e: Native VLAN on an unused VLAN (999) prevents double tagging.
explain.c: The uplink between switches carries several VLANs: trunk.
explain.f: nonegotiate turns DTP off: nobody forms a trunk with this port by negotiation.

chips.why: Host port mode: a single VLAN.
Port mode between switches: several tagged VLANs.
Tries to form a trunk via DTP with whoever is on the other side. That's exactly what enables switch spoofing.
VLAN 1 is the factory default. Using it as native or for hosts is the classic mistake.
Explicit list of the VLANs allowed on the trunk.
Allowing all takes to the core even VLANs that shouldn't leave this switch.
A VLAN with no users: a good choice for native VLAN.
Turns DTP off on the port.
Port-security limits the MACs accepted on the port. It's useful, but it doesn't turn DTP off.

levels.title: Broken uplink
levels.goal: Find the cut, understand why the redundancy failed and bring the backup path back.
levels.z: I cut the path to the 3rd floor. And that backup cable of yours? Hahaha.
levels.me: If there's a backup, there's a way out. First I find the cut.
levels.intro: The whole 3rd floor disappeared from monitoring. Test from the datacenter MONITOR. No traceroute this time: it either answers or it doesn't. The dashed link is the backup.
lesson: Without traceroute, you only know whether each destination answers or not. Compare the results to corner the fault.
Redundancy: the access switch has two uplinks, one to each core switch. If one cable goes down, the other takes over.
STP (Spanning Tree) keeps the backup link blocked to avoid a loop and releases it when the main one goes down. With RSTP, in a few seconds.
A port in shutdown was turned off by the administrator. It doesn't take over anything on its own.
levels.tip: Ping SW-CORE-1, the internet and SW-ANDAR3. Whatever answers is on the datacenter side. Floor 3 is behind cable Gi0/1.
levels.learn: Redundancy only protects if it's active: the backup uplink was in shutdown, so cutting Gi0/1 isolated the floor. With both uplinks up, STP (RSTP) blocks one and releases it in seconds when the other goes down. Monitor both links to know when you're running without a backup.

nodes.why: One of the 3rd-floor PCs. It depends on SW-ANDAR3 to talk to anything.
3rd-floor access switch. It has two uplinks: Gi0/1 to SW-CORE-1 and Gi0/2 (backup) to SW-CORE-2.
Main core switch. It concentrates the floors, the servers and the exit.
Backup core switch, connected to the main core. It's the one that would take floor 3 if Gi0/2 were active.
Edge router: the exit to the internet.
Datacenter server, hanging off the main core.

links.why: This is the backup link, turned off (dashed). It didn't go down now: it was already out. It's part of the problem, but it isn't the cut.

levels.faultName: On uplink Gi0/1 between SW-ANDAR3 and SW-CORE-1
levels.faultWhy: The monitor reaches both cores, the edge, the internet and the server, but nothing on floor 3. The cut is on uplink Gi0/1 between SW-ANDAR3 and SW-CORE-1. The floor switch's console log confirms it: Gi0/1 down. Since the backup was in shutdown, nobody took over.

steps.q: Why didn't the backup link (Gi0/2) save floor 3?
v: If there was a backup link (Gi0/2), why did floor 3 go down?
Floor 3 had a second uplink. Why didn't it take over?
o: The backup port was in shutdown: redundancy that's turned off doesn't protect

o.t: STP blocks the backup link forever
o.why: STP blocks the backup only while the main one is up. When the main one goes down, it releases the backup.

o.t: A backup link only works with BGP
o.why: Between switches on the same network, redundancy is handled by STP (or link aggregation). BGP is between networks (ASes).

steps.why: Redundancy has to be active and tested. With STP, the backup stays blocked and takes over on its own when the main one goes down. In shutdown, it never takes over.

steps.q: Through SW-ANDAR3's console cable, how do you bring backup port Gi0/2 back up?
v: On SW-ANDAR3's console, which commands bring Gi0/2 back up?
Connected to SW-ANDAR3's console, how do you re-enable backup port Gi0/2?
o: interface gi0/2 and then no shutdown

o.t: interface gi0/2 and then spanning-tree portfast
o.why: PortFast is for user ports (it speeds up link-up). On a port between switches it risks a loop, and the port would stay off.
shutdown turns the port off. It's the opposite of what you want.

steps.why: no shutdown turns the port on. STP negotiates and floor 3 comes back through SW-CORE-2.

steps.q: So the next cut doesn't take the floor down, the right move is:
v: So a future cut doesn't take the floor down, what's the best practice?
How do you really protect floor 3 against losing an uplink?
o: Keep both uplinks up with STP (or LACP aggregation) and monitor both

o.t: Turn off STP so both uplinks forward together
o.why: Without STP, two paths between switches form a loop: a broadcast storm takes the network down in seconds.

o.t: Use a single uplink, on pricier fiber
o.why: A single cable is a single point of failure, whatever the price.

steps.why: Two active, watched paths. STP prevents the loop; aggregation (LACP) uses both at the same time when they connect to the same pair of switches.

levels.title: BGP customer filter
levels.cap: Opening the BGP session with customer AS64500...
levels.goal: Decide what to accept from BGP customer AS64500, owner of block 45.160.0.0/22.
levels.intro: Customer AS64500 has block 45.160.0.0/22 with a ROA up to /24. Accept only what's theirs. The rest is a leak or a hijack.
levels.z: I'll announce whatever I want through your customer. You accept everything anyway.
levels.me: A BGP customer only announces what's theirs. Strict prefix-list.
lesson: BGP is the protocol the internet's networks (each with its own AS number) use to exchange routes. Each AS announces the blocks it owns.
BGP trusts what the neighbor announces. If you accept everything from the customer, a mistake or attack on their side becomes a problem for the whole internet.
A prefix-list says exactly what to accept. 45.160.0.0/22 le 24 = the /22 and any piece of it up to /24.
The /22 goes from 45.160.0.0 to 45.160.3.255. Most of the internet drops prefixes more specific than /24, and the ROA (RPKI) records who can announce the block and up to what size.
Never accept from a customer: a default route, private or reserved ranges (bogons), your blocks or third-party blocks.
levels.tip: 45.160.0.0/22 covers 45.160.0.0 to 45.160.3.255. Accept only prefixes inside that between /22 and /24. Default route, bogons, your own prefixes and third-party blocks are rejected.
levels.learn: Customer filter = prefix-list 45.160.0.0/22 le 24. Reject default, RFC 1918, CGNAT, your own blocks and anything more specific than /24, which the internet drops. Add max-prefix and RPKI validation to close the net. That's what MANRS asks for.

a.why: The customer's whole block, exactly as registered.
Half of the /22 (45.160.0 and 45.160.1): inside the block and not beyond /24.
A /24 inside the /22 (45.160.0 to 45.160.3), allowed by the ROA.
The last /24 of the block, still inside 45.160.0.0/22.
Default route. A customer should never announce a default to the provider.
RFC 1918 private range (bogon). It doesn't travel on the internet.
It's YOUR block. Accepting it from the customer would divert your own traffic to them.
Google's block. The customer doesn't own it: it would be a prefix hijack.
The /22 ends at 45.160.3.255. 45.160.4 is already outside the customer's block.
/25 is more specific than the /24 the ROA allows: it would be RPKI invalid.

levels.title: Prefix hijack
levels.cap: Route alert on the BGP dashboard...
levels.goal: Z3R0 is announcing your prefixes on the internet. Find out how he does it and how to defend.
levels.z: I announced a /24 out of your /22 out there. All your traffic goes through me now.
levels.me: Longest match. I'm closing that gap.
lesson: In the routing table the most specific prefix always wins (longest prefix match). A /24 beats a /22, whatever the AS-path.
Hijack: someone announces a prefix that isn't theirs. If the announcement is more specific than yours, the traffic goes to them.
RPKI: the block owner publishes a ROA saying which AS may announce it and the maximum size (maxLength). Whoever does ROV drops invalid announcements.
ROV only checks the origin and the size. It doesn't check the path: whoever forges your AS as the origin gets through. That's what ASPA is for.
Route leak: a customer passes on routes it learned from others. maximum-prefix drops the session if it announces more than agreed.
levels.tip: The router always prefers the most specific prefix. RPKI validates origin and maximum size, but not the path.
levels.learn: A hijack with a more specific prefix wins by longest prefix match. A ROA with maxLength equal to the real announcement makes the fake /24 RPKI invalid, and whoever does ROV drops it. A forged origin passes RPKI; that's where ASPA and transit filters come in. Max-prefix protects against a customer route leak.

qs.q: You announce 177.10.0.0/22. Z3R0 announces 177.10.1.0/24 from another AS. Where does traffic for 177.10.1.5 go?
v: You announce 177.10.0.0/22 and Z3R0 announces 177.10.1.0/24 from another AS. Where does traffic to 177.10.1.5 go?
Your /22 against Z3R0's /24 inside it. Who gets the traffic to 177.10.1.5?
o: To Z3R0, because the /24 is more specific

o.t: To you, because you announced first
o.why: Announcement order doesn't matter between different prefixes. The most specific wins.

o.t: To whoever has the shorter AS-path
o.why: AS-path only breaks ties between routes for the SAME prefix. /24 and /22 are different routes.
There's no split: for each destination, the table picks the most specific prefix.

qs.why: Longest prefix match comes before any BGP attribute. The /24 beats the /22.

qs.q: Z3R0 can forge your AS as the origin. Which ROA still makes a /24 inside your /22 invalid?
v: Even with Z3R0 forging your origin AS, which ROA makes a /24 inside your /22 invalid?
Which ROA makes any /24 taken from your /22 invalid, even with your AS forged as the origin?

o.why: maxLength /24 authorizes announcements up to /24. A /24 with your forged origin would be valid.
Without a ROA the state is "not found", and almost nobody drops not-found routes.
It authorizes any piece of the block, down to /32. The opposite of what you want.

qs.why: With maxLength /22, any announcement more specific than /22 is invalid, even with the right origin.

qs.q: If Z3R0 announces the /22 forging YOUR AS as the origin, does RPKI ROV detect it?
v: Z3R0 announces your /22 with YOUR AS forged as the origin. Does RPKI ROV catch it?
A route with the same prefix and origin AS as yours, but coming through Z3R0. Does ROV mark it invalid?
o: No. ROV only validates origin and size, not the path

o.why: ROV only compares the origin AS and the size with the ROA. If the forged origin matches, the route is valid.

o.t: Yes, if it has a community
o.why: A community is just a tag on the route. It isn't part of RPKI validation.
RPKI works the same way for IPv4 and IPv6.

qs.why: A forged origin passes ROV. That's why ASPA, BGPsec and transit filters exist.

qs.q: Your BGP customer leaked the full table (900 thousand routes) to you. What would have dropped the session before the damage?
v: A BGP customer sent you the full table (900 thousand routes) by mistake. Which setting would have dropped the session earlier?
Full-table leak from a BGP customer. Which protection on the session would have prevented the damage?

o.why: It helps the router survive, but traffic would still be diverted through the leaked routes.
no-export limits how far routes are passed on. It doesn't stop you from receiving them.
High local-preference would make you PREFER the leaked routes. It would only make it worse.

qs.why: Max-prefix drops the session when the customer goes over the agreed limit. Basic protection against route leaks.
